gaps.title: Dynamic intended use / behavioral envelope
gaps.explanation: GenAI systems may move between informational, recommendatory, and action-directing behavior over the course of a conversation.

examples.excerpt: In our pilot the same assistant summarized, then recommended, then produced an order draft, all in one exchange.
A patient reading a confident paragraph does not see an informational feature. They see an instruction.
Say what the system is allowed to do, in a list, in the labeling.

gaps.title: Human-AI system performance
gaps.explanation: The clinically relevant unit of performance may often be the combined human-AI system rather than the model alone.

examples.excerpt: Benchmark performance and bedside performance have not matched in any deployment we have reviewed.
The question is not whether the model is right. It is whether a tired clinician at hour ten will notice when it is not.
We can characterize the tool under representative use. We cannot warrant a staffing model.

gaps.title: Deployment assurance & scalability
gaps.explanation: The same product may perform differently across populations, workflows, EHR configurations, local data, users, and safeguards. FDA needs a clearer framework for what manufacturers establish globally and what deploying organizations must validate locally.

examples.excerpt: Site-by-site surveillance of every deployment is not a program. It is a headcount problem with no ceiling.
The first signal we received was a nurse saying the summaries had started sounding different.
Same product, same version, two hospitals, materially different output quality.

gaps.title: Operational harm
gaps.explanation: Over-escalation, rework, unnecessary utilization, clinician burden, and workflow disruption may matter even where classic device harm is absent.

examples.excerpt: A prospective study for a discharge summary drafting aid costs more than the product will ever return.
We are willing to monitor. We are not willing to staff someone else's compliance program.
Sample-based review by independent clinicians is a good idea with no line item.

gaps.title: Evidence burden & commercial viability
gaps.explanation: Continuous benchmarking and clinical validation can improve assurance, but regulatory obligations may become economically unscalable if they are not proportional to risk and product value.

examples.excerpt: We can build to a demanding standard. We cannot build to an unstated one.
A prospective study for a discharge summary drafting aid costs more than the product will ever return.
Every unstated requirement shows up in our models as a discount on the round.

gaps.title: AI supplier quality
gaps.explanation: Foundation model companies function increasingly like critical suppliers whose changes can alter regulated product behavior.

examples.excerpt: We can plan our own releases. The base model changed twice during our submission review.
The supplier control framework already exists. It was written for parts that do not change themselves.
We can commit to telling customers when behavior changes. We cannot open the training corpus.

gaps.title: Cybersecurity as clinical safety
gaps.explanation: Prompt injection, tool manipulation, retrieval poisoning, and related vulnerabilities can become direct clinical hazards.

examples.excerpt: A retrieval poisoning event is not an IT incident. It is a clinical one.
Red-teaming without a reported matrix is an anecdote, not evidence.
The documents that poisoned our pilot were our own. No sponsor could have tested against them.

gaps.title: Distributed accountability
gaps.explanation: Manufacturers, foundation-model developers, platform vendors, health systems, and clinicians may each control different parts of the safety system.

examples.excerpt: We are willing to monitor. We are not willing to staff someone else's compliance program.
Every deployment should have a name attached to it before go-live.
The liability sits with us and the visibility sits with them.

gaps.title: Delegated authority
gaps.explanation: Agentic systems raise a distinct question: what actions has the organization actually delegated to the AI, and how far can an error propagate before meaningful human intervention?

examples.excerpt: A wrong sentence is a draft. A wrong action is an event.
Nobody in our organization signed a document saying the assistant could do that.
Say what the system is allowed to do, in a list, in the labeling.
